content: The guidelines for diagnosing, preventing, and managing cryptococcal disease among adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV were developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2022. These guidelines are intended to provide evidence-based recommendations for healthcare professionals to improve outcomes for individuals affected by this condition. Below is a detailed explanation of the key terms and concepts used in the guidelines, as well as the processes and contributors involved in their development. 1. Age Groups: An adult is defined as a person older than 19 years of age. An adolescent is a person aged 10–19 years, inclusive. A child is a person aged 1 year to younger than 10 years. An infant is a child younger than 1 year of age. 2. Advanced HIV Disease: For adults, adolescents, and children aged 5 years or older, advanced HIV disease is defined as a CD4 cell count of less than 200 cells/mm³ or the presence of a WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 event at the time of presentation for care. All children living with HIV who are younger than 5 years should be considered as having advanced HIV disease at presentation. 3. Cryptococcal Antigen Positivity: This refers to the detection of cryptococcal antigen in serum, plasma, or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). A positive CSF antigen test indicates cryptococcal meningitis. 4. Cryptococcal Disease: This is an infection caused by Cryptococcus species that impairs normal body function. It is identified through abnormal clinical symptoms or signs. 5. Cryptococcal Infection: This is the growth of Cryptococcus species in the body, documented either by direct culture of the organism or indirect detection (e.g., a positive antigen test in a person without prior cryptococcal disease or an India ink stain). A positive culture or the first positive antigen test typically indicates active disease. 6. Cryptococcoma: This is a localized, solid, tumor-like mass caused by the growth of the cryptococcal organism and an associated inflammatory response. It can occur intracranially or extracranially. 7. Cryptococcus Species: The most common species causing human disease in the context of HIV infection is Cryptococcus neoformans. Cryptococcus gattii can also occur in this context, and the resulting disease is indistinguishable from that caused by C. neoformans. 8. Meningeal Disease: This refers to a disease presenting with nervous system signs or symptoms, specifically involving the meningeal layer surrounding the brain. 9. Microbiological Culture-Positive Relapse: This is a new episode of active disease following the resolution of a previous episode. 10. Non-Meningeal Disease: This refers to disease that does not involve the brain but affects either a single site in the body (localized) or two non-contiguous sites in the body (disseminated). 11. Persistent Symptoms: These are symptoms consistent with cryptococcal disease that fail to resolve after two weeks of initial antifungal induction treatment. 12. Raised Intracranial Pressure: This is defined as a cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure of ≥25 cm H₂O. 13. Recurrent Symptoms: These are symptoms consistent with cryptococcal disease that reappear after full resolution following treatment for the initial episode of cryptococcal meningitis. 14. Suboptimal Treatment: This refers to treatment with an inadequate drug regimen, dose, or duration of induction, consolidation, or maintenance therapy. It may also result from drug interactions or drug resistance. 15. Sustained Clinical Response: This is defined as the resolution of clinical symptoms and signs of cryptococcal disease for at least two continuous weeks. 16. Treatment Failure: This is the lack of clinical or mycological response among individuals who received suboptimal treatment or who received optimal treatment but failed to respond clinically. The guidelines were developed through a rigorous process involving contributions from a wide range of experts, including clinicians, researchers, and public health professionals. The development process included systematic reviews of evidence, consultations with stakeholders, and consideration of ethical and cost-related factors. The WHO acknowledges the contributions of numerous individuals and organizations in updating these guidelines, including members of the Guideline Development Group, external reviewers, and technical advisors. The guidelines emphasize the importance of evidence-based practices in managing cryptococcal disease, particularly in the context of HIV infection. They also highlight the need for ongoing research, dissemination of updated recommendations, and collaboration among healthcare providers to improve patient outcomes.
